done.why: I had seen enough of the prose to rate it and stopped early, with no ending reached.

about: A cave-crawl in the Colossal Cave tradition. You start in a barrow with a lantern and an Elvish sword, cross a ravine, and head into a cavern system. A Wizard says that the treasures lie south of the ravine, and his words can conjure things that aren't there.

moments.note: The lantern is described as 'a thing that has been through one adventure already and would rather not discuss it'.
Turning on the lamp made the Wizard appear. His look at my empty hands was written as if he were reading me.
The conjured yellow sphere turns out to be nothing, and the room 'has the grace to look embarrassed about it now'.
A grue was listed at the Shallow Ford, then the room 'settles down and is only a room'. That was my guess at it being another illusion, and nothing confirmed it.

wished: More time to see where the Wizard's illusions lead.
A way to ask the Wizard something.

lines.line: It has that look of a thing that has been through one adventure already and would rather not discuss it.
lines.why: Wry, and it lets the lantern carry the weight of earlier adventures.

lines.line: It was never there: the Wizard's word put it in the room, and the room, having no say in the matter, let it, and has the grace to look embarrassed about it now.
lines.why: Gives the room a personality and explains the illusion elegantly.

lines.line: He peers at you from under his bushy eyebrows, as though you were not at all what he had been expecting, and had turned up anyway.
lines.why: Characterful reaction text that responds to the player.

fun.why: Playful responses and a little mystery, though I only played a short while.

engagement.why: The Wizard and his illusions made me want to look further.

difficulty.why: Nothing blocked me in the short stretch I played.

interestingness.why: It reworks the old cave setting with a Wizard who conjures false objects, and the lantern seems to recall earlier adventures.

prose.why: Dry, witty, and personified. Even the failure messages read as prose worth reading.
